clinicalPearls: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the single most common cause of acute liver failure, and hepatotoxicity signals are the leading reason candidate compounds fail to gain approval during drug development; a meticulous history covering prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, dietary, occupational and household chemical exposures is essential (Harrison 22e p.2665).

Two broad categories are recognized: direct (intrinsic) toxic injury, which is predictable, dose-dependent and has a short latency (often hours), and idiosyncratic injury, which is infrequent (roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100,000 exposures), less clearly dose-related and typically appears 5-90 days after starting the drug (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666).

The R value, the ratio of ALT to alkaline phosphatase (each as a multiple of the upper limit of normal), classifies the injury pattern: R greater than 5 indicates hepatocellular injury, R less than 2 indicates cholestatic injury, and R of 2-5 indicates a mixed pattern (Harrison 22e p.2667).

Hy's Law, named for Hyman Zimmerman, holds that drug-induced jaundice during a trial predicts serious liver injury, with roughly a 10-to-1 ratio of jaundiced cases to cases of acute liver failure; such cases often portend failure of drug approval (Harrison 22e p.2667).

Acetaminophen is the prototypic direct hepatotoxin and the most prevalent cause of acute liver failure in the Western world; it produces dose-related centrilobular necrosis, and aminotransferases can exceed 10,000 IU/L, far above levels seen in viral hepatitis, often with a relatively low bilirubin in this hyperacute injury (Harrison 22e p.2668).

A characteristic biochemical clue to acetaminophen toxicity is the combination of extremely high aminotransferases with low bilirubin; clinical suspicion should prompt empiric N-acetylcysteine even before history is confirmed, since denial or altered mentation can obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2668).

Isoniazid causes transient mild aminotransferase elevation in about 10% of recipients early in therapy (an 'adaptive' response that usually resolves despite continued use); clinically significant hepatocellular injury can appear over a latency of up to 6 months and rises sharply with age, being highest in those over 50 and lowest in those under 20 (Harrison 22e p.2670).

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the most commonly implicated single agent in DILI in the United States and Europe, producing a fairly specific mixed or predominantly cholestatic injury that may begin after the drug has already been stopped owing to a long latency (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671).

Complementary and alternative medicines, including herbal and dietary weight-loss and body-building products, now account for more than 20% of DILI cases in the United States; implicated agents include green tea extract (Camellia sinensis), kava, germander, chaparral, comfrey (pyrrolizidine alkaloids), Hydroxycut and OxyElite Pro (Harrison 22e p.2671).

Certain drugs produce an autoimmune-hepatitis-like phenotype with positive antinuclear antibodies, classically nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine and alpha-methyldopa (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671).

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab; anti-PD-1 pembrolizumab and nivolumab) cause an immune-mediated hepatitis within weeks, often ANA-positive, mediated predominantly by CD8+ lymphocytes and responsive to glucocorticoids; concurrent immune injury to thyroid, muscle and colon may occur (Harrison 22e p.2671-2672).

Withdrawal of the suspected agent at the first sign of an adverse reaction, or when aminotransferases reach five times the upper limit of normal, is critical, because continued use despite symptoms and signs is associated with lethal outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2668).
harrison.pathophysiology: Hepatotoxicity arises from direct hepatocyte injury (free radicals or reactive metabolites causing membrane lipid peroxidation) or from drug/metabolite activation of innate or adaptive immune pathways, apoptotic signaling, and disruption of bile excretory transport. Interference with canalicular pumps allows injurious endogenous bile acids to accumulate, producing cholestasis; other mechanisms inhibit protein synthesis or impair mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, leading to lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Most drugs are metabolized via phase I cytochrome P450 (oxidation) followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation; most toxicity reflects formation of a reactive phase I metabolite, with glutathione depletion removing a protective pathway. For acetaminophen, phase II conjugation yields harmless metabolites, but a fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic intermediate NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione; when glutathione is overwhelmed or depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive necrosis. Susceptibility to idiosyncratic injury is influenced by HLA haplotypes (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin), polymorphisms in metabolizing pathways and protective cytokines, and activation of nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR. Factors potentiating acetaminophen injury include enzyme induction (alcohol via CYP2E1, phenobarbital, isoniazid), fasting/starvation and other states that lower hepatic glutathione (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666, 2668-2670).
additionalDifferentials: Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C) - idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI can be clinically and histologically indistinguishable
Autoimmune hepatitis (especially with nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa)
Alcoholic hepatitis (amiodarone produces a pseudoalcoholic picture)
Biliary obstruction and primary sclerosing cholangitis (DILI can mimic sclerosing cholangitis after floxuridine or long-term ketamine)
Cholestasis of pregnancy (shares genetic canalicular transporter defects with estrogen-induced cholestasis)
infectionMimics: Acute viral hepatitis A, B, and C
additionalInvestigations: Serial ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin to define pattern and compute the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of upper limit of normal)
Serum acetaminophen level timed 4-8 h after ingestion, interpreted against the treatment nomogram (levels above 300 mcg/mL at 4 h predict severe injury; below 150 mcg/mL injury unlikely)
Acetaminophen-protein (acetaminophen-Cys) adduct measurement by HPLC as an investigational diagnostic marker
Arterial blood lactate in acute liver failure (above 3.5 mmol/L suggests likely need for transplantation)
Autoantibodies (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-LKM2, anti-mitochondrial) when an autoimmune-pattern or checkpoint-inhibitor injury is suspected
Liver biopsy when the pattern is uncertain (may show centrilobular necrosis, microvesicular steatosis, granulomas, phospholipid-laden lamellar bodies in amiodarone, or vanishing bile ducts)
Exclusion of viral, autoimmune and biliary causes; structured causality assessment (DILIN expert opinion, RUCAM, or newer RECAM)
redFlags: Jaundice arising during drug exposure (Hy's Law) predicts serious injury and possible liver failure
Coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy - markers of acute liver failure, which develops in about 10% of DILI cases
Aminotransferases above 10,000 IU/L with a low bilirubin - hyperacute acetaminophen pattern
Continued ingestion despite nausea, fatigue or jaundice (common scenario in fatal isoniazid and acetaminophen toxicity)
Acetaminophen ingestion of 25 g or more, or high timed plasma levels on the nomogram
Arterial lactate above 3.5 mmol/L in acetaminophen acute liver failure
Concurrent renal failure or myocardial injury in acetaminophen overdose
harrison.prognosis: Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after withdrawal of the offending agent. Acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and over 40% of those patients undergo liver transplantation. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have lasting liver injury, though the associated acute kidney injury (seen in nearly 75% of severe cases) is almost always self-limited. Anabolic steroid cholestasis typically resolves over weeks to months with prolonged jaundice. Some agents cause chronic injury: methotrexate, tamoxifen and amiodarone can lead to cirrhosis, and several drugs cause chronic autoimmune-like hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.2668-2670).
pitfalls: DILI is nearly always a diagnosis of exclusion; causality is hard to prove and many disorders produce an identical clinicopathologic picture
Mild transient aminotransferase elevations that resolve during continued therapy ('adaptation,' seen with isoniazid, valproate, phenytoin and statins) can be mistaken for significant toxicity
Long latency drugs (notably amoxicillin-clavulanate and nitrofurantoin) may cause injury that manifests only after the drug has been stopped
Idiosyncratic reactions occurring in under 1 in 10,000 recipients are missed by clinical trials and only detected through postmarketing surveillance (e.g., troglitazone)
In chronic alcohol users, glutathione depletion and CYP2E1 induction can make the toxic acetaminophen dose as low as 2 g
Activated charcoal or cholestyramine are ineffective if given more than 30 minutes after acetaminophen ingestion
Routine liver test monitoring during statin therapy is not recommended, and asymptomatic isolated aminotransferase elevations need not prompt discontinuation
Herbal/dietary supplements may contain undeclared pharmaceuticals (e.g., diclofenac in antirheumatic 'herbs'), so the history must specifically probe alternative-medicine use
harrison.severityClassification: Injury pattern is graded by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): hepatocellular (R > 5), cholestatic (R < 2), or mixed (R 2-5). Severity is judged clinically by progression to acute liver failure (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy). Causality likelihood is assessed by structured tools including the DILIN expert-opinion scale (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely), RUCAM, and the newer RECAM. Hy's Law identifies high-risk hepatocellular injury when jaundice accompanies hepatocellular enzyme elevation (Harrison 22e p.2667-2668).
management: Immediate withdrawal of the suspected offending drug or toxin as the essential first step
N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol toxicity, given empirically when suspected without awaiting confirmation
Supportive care with correction of fluid, electrolyte, and metabolic derangement, and cholestyramine for cholestatic pruritus
Corticosteroids for hypersensitivity or autoimmune-pattern injury, including checkpoint-inhibitor hepatitis
Serial monitoring of transaminases, bilirubin, and coagulation, watching for the coagulopathy and encephalopathy that herald acute liver failure
Early referral to a specialist liver and transplant centre for acute liver failure, with consideration of emergency transplantation
Document the reaction and counsel the patient to avoid re-exposure to the causative agent and related compounds
